flight planning (submit a completed DD-1: Flight Planning, DD-1801, and Jet Log

overview: I4490 is the instrument check-flight preparation event. The standard is to show examiner-ready judgment: the flight plan is complete, current data is checked, lost-communications and weather-minimum decisions are defensible, and prior instrument procedures can be explained without leaning on local gouge.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Lost communications should be briefed as a predictable plan that ATC can protect, with PIC emergency authority available when the rule does not fit the actual safety problem.

children.text: If the failure occurs in VFR conditions, or VFR conditions are encountered after the failure, continue under VFR and land as soon as practicable.
Land as soon as practicable does not mean land immediately at an unsuitable field, and the VFR branch also applies if the failure occurs in Class A.
Squawk 7600 and attempt recontact on the last assigned frequency, FSS, New York Radio or San Francisco Radio, 121.5 MHz, and NAVAID voice as able.
For IFR route, use AVE-F: assigned, vectored direct to the specified fix/route/airway, expected, then filed.
For IFR altitude, use AME for each segment: highest of assigned altitude, minimum IFR altitude, or expected altitude.
Make MEA, MCA, MRA, and valid EFC-altitude changes at the appropriate segment, time, or fix; do not apply an expected altitude before it becomes usable.
If the clearance limit is a fix from which an approach begins, begin descent or approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or ETA if no EFC was received.
If the clearance limit is not an approach fix, leave it at EFC time, or on arrival if no EFC was received, then proceed to a fix from which an approach begins.

For radar approaches, brief the specific lost-communication interval and backup plan: secondary or tower frequency, VFR if possible, approved non-radar approach, or the radar approach's published lost-communication procedure.

items.text: CNAF minimums are the check-flight weather gates: can the aircraft legally depart, may the approach be commenced, and may it continue below MDA or DH.

children.text: For a standard instrument rating, a non-precision-supported takeoff requires the published minimums for the available approach, but not less than a 300-foot ceiling and 1 SM visibility.
If a compatible precision approach is available and usable for the landing runway, takeoff may use those precision minimums, but never below 200-foot ceiling and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
A special instrument rating has no takeoff ceiling or visibility minimums, but only an aircraft commander with that rating, on the flight controls, may depart below the applicable minimums.
Use approved DoD FLIP or equivalent procedures. For straight-in approaches, RVR governs when available; for circling, prevailing visibility governs.
A single-piloted aircraft shall not commence an instrument approach if reported weather is below published minimums for the type of approach being conducted.
The fixed-wing single-pilot absolute floor is 200-foot ceiling or HAT and 1/2 SM visibility or 2400 RVR.
Do not descend below MDA or continue below DH unless the runway environment is in sight and a safe landing can be made.
On a precision approach, execute the missed approach at DH if the runway environment is not in sight or a safe landing cannot be made.
On a non-precision approach, execute the missed at the MAP if visual reference is not established or the landing cannot be accomplished.
If visual reference is lost while circling, start with a climbing turn toward the landing runway, then maneuver the shortest direction to join the published missed-approach course.

items.text: The check flight requires a completed DD-1801, DD-1801-C stopover plan, and jet log that agree with each other and with the weather, NOTAM, fuel, alternate, and delay plan.

children.text: CNAF preflight planning requires familiarity with weather reports and forecasts, NOTAMs, TFRs, fuel requirements, terminal procedures, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, anticipated traffic delays, and risk.
The DD-1801 is the formal IFR flight-plan request; the jet log is the cockpit math that proves headings, distances, ETEs, fuel burns, EFRs, alternate fuel, and DRAFT data.
Build the route and fuel story from the same assumptions: fuel aboard, start/taxi/takeoff fuel, climb and cruise profile, approach fuel, alternate fuel, reserve, and spare fuel.
Use DD-1801 for the initial leg and DD-1801-C for subsequent legs in a stopover flight plan.
The DD-1801-C uses the same completion guidance as DD-1801, can support three additional legs, and carries new fuel endurance and persons on board in Block 19 for each leg.
Use Block 18 on the DD-1801-C only when information changes from the initial DD-1801.
For an en route holding delay, use DLE/ with the significant point on the route followed by the delay length in four-digit hours and minutes.
For a terminal delay, show the practice instrument approach delay in the route structure so ATC can see the intended terminal work.
For this event, the first leg should include the en route holding delay and the second leg should include the terminal delay; the jet log must carry the fuel and timing consequences of both.

sections.title: Flight Planning, DD-1801, and Jet Log

items.text: NOTAMs are time-critical aeronautical information that can change whether the planned route, procedure, airport, NAVAID, airspace, or GPS plan is usable.

children.text: For DoD operations, use DAIP when available; if DAIP is unavailable, get a NOTAM briefing through FSS by phone or other approved means.
Check departure, destination, alternate, route, ARTCCs along the route, TFRs, special-use airspace activity, and any GPS/RAIM issue that affects the planned procedures.
If a location is not covered by the U.S. NOTAM system, use FSS or direct airport contact as needed.
NOTAM(D) can cover airport, taxiway, lighting, and facility status that may not change approach criteria but still affects execution.
FDC NOTAMs are regulatory and may amend instrument procedures, published charts, or advertise TFRs.
Pointer NOTAMs point to another NOTAM; SAA NOTAMs activate special-activity airspace; military NOTAMs cover military NAVAIDs and airports in the NAS.
Domestic and International Notices are not included in a standard FSS briefing unless requested, so ask for them if they have not already been reviewed.
CNAF makes FLIP procedures, special notices, instructions, and NOTAMs mandatory for naval aircraft pilots.
A check-flight NOTAM answer should end with a cockpit effect: procedure unavailable, alternate invalid, NAVAID unusable, airspace unavailable, timing changed, or no factor.

items.text: En route weather is not a one-time preflight snapshot; it is the in-flight update loop that protects the route, destination, alternate, and fuel plan.

children.text: Use PMSV/METRO, FSS, ARTCC weather advisories, ATIS, ASOS/AWSS, AWOS, UNICOM/AUNICOM, ATC weather avoidance assistance, and PIREPs as the route develops.
ARTCC may broadcast the availability of severe weather forecast alerts, convective SIGMETs, SIGMETs, AIRMETs, urgent PIREPs, and CWA information affecting their area.
FSS specialists may brief and interpret available reports and forecasts, but they are not original forecasters.
PMSV/METRO can update weather information, help with DD-175-1 updates, and receive PIREPs for rapid dissemination.
Compare each update against approach minimums, alternate requirements, fuel-to-alternate, severe weather watches, SIGMETs, icing, thunderstorms, turbulence, and route delays.
If the DD-175-1 void time, weather briefed time, route, or delay plan no longer supports the flight, update the plan before the check flight becomes a fuel or legality problem.
Use ATC weather avoidance assistance for precipitation information, but remember ATC radar does not detect turbulence and NEXRAD-based products can be delayed.
Give PIREPs for hazardous weather and useful cloud, visibility, icing, turbulence, wind shear, or precipitation observations.

items.text: Any emergency procedure in a check-flight event is a cumulative oral evaluation of judgment, not just a memory-item recital.

children.text: State the cue, maintain aircraft control, execute required immediate action, back it up with the checklist, and identify the N/W/C that changes the branch.
Tie the procedure to the phase of flight: departure obstacle clearance, en route weather, lost communications, fuel state, approach minimums, alternate selection, or recovery-field suitability.
Finish with the branch: continue, land as soon as practical, land as soon as possible, PEL, forced landing, or eject.
If the emergency affects IFR capability, tell ATC what failed, what capability remains, and what clearance or vectors are needed.
Do not invent an exhaustive EP list for the event. Be prepared to apply the same method to whichever NATOPS EP the instructor selects.

Common check-flight misses are treating a warning as a note, troubleshooting below the useful altitude band, delaying ejection past a limit, or forgetting that a systems failure can invalidate the IFR plan.

items.text: Any previously discussed item means the check flight can reach back across the instrument syllabus; prepare prior events as linked procedures rather than isolated flash facts.

children.text: For each prior item, know the purpose, setup, clearance meaning, numbers or gates, execution flow, common error, missed or lost-communication branch, and source.

High-value review lanes are scan and basic instrument maneuvers, holding, course intercepts, PAR/ASR/no-gyro, ILS/LOC, GPS/RNAV/TAA, SID/STAR, ODP/Trouble T, fuel management, DD-1801/jet log, NOTAMs, and weather.
If a question is local or scenario-specific, answer from the current chart, IFG, ATC clearance, or local procedure for that day; do not rely on stale route names or memorized frequencies.
A strong check-flight answer ends in a cockpit action: what you would set, brief, request, fly, verify, or discontinue.

studyNotes.summary: Brief the check flight as one integrated standard: legal launch, complete DD-1801/jet log, current NOTAM and weather picture, lost-communications plan, EP branch logic, and source-backed review of prior instrument items.

summary: Instrument check-flight planning, lost communications, weather minimums, NOTAMs, en route weather, EPs, and cumulative review.
